text: The most common objection to the last two lessons is a reasonable one: isn't this just like two coins secretly prepared to match? That's not spooky, that's just correlation. This lesson takes that objection seriously — and shows exactly where it stops working.

Here's the skeptic's model, stated precisely: two coins prepared in advance carrying the same hidden instruction, a secret script each carries wherever it goes. This is a local hidden variable model — local because nothing needs to travel between the coins at measurement time. This isn't a silly idea; it's exactly what Einstein, Podolsky, and Rosen proposed in 1935. Checked against the same fixed question every time, a hidden script reproduces correlation perfectly.

Recall that measuring Phi-plus in the computational basis gives P of 00 and P of 11 each 0.5, and P of 01 and P of 10 exactly zero. A script — write 0 on both coins half the time, 1 the other half — produces exactly this pattern too. If the computational basis were the only way anyone ever measured a Bell pair, there'd be no way to distinguish genuine entanglement from two coins carrying a shared secret.

The reason entanglement isn't reducible to a shared script is that quantum mechanics lets you measure in different bases — rotated angles, not just the computational one. A script has to commit in advance to an answer for every basis someone might later choose, since it's fixed before the particles separate. It turns out no fixed script, however cleverly designed, can reproduce the correlations quantum mechanics predicts once you compare measurements at multiple different angles. The quantum correlations are measurably stronger than any classical shared-randomness scheme once more than one measurement setting is in play.
Next lesson delivers the precise numeric test for this gap — the CHSH inequality, the same test that won a Nobel Prize and now underpins real cryptographic protocols.
